questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I decided to go on exchange in Oslo because it's within Europe, and I find it exciting to connect with other young people from across the Nordic region and Europe. Oslo is home to a highly regarded university with a renowned anthropology faculty, which was a major draw for me. On top of that, Norway's stunning landscapes offer a unique natural beauty that we simply don't have in Denmark.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I found it very easy to access the information I needed, both before and after arriving in Oslo. The university's administration was highly approachable and responsive, and my accommodation was managed directly from the same campus where I studied. Everything was well-organized and intuitive, making the whole process seamless.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I received great support with arranging my accommodation, obtaining a student card, and discovering the introductory activities for exchange students on my campus. Additionally, I was guided on how to navigate the teaching portals and access course materials, which made settling in much easier.

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Finding accommodation off-campus was straightforward. I used the SIO service, which manages all student housing in Oslo. I know that all the other exchange students I got to know also used it, and it worked really well. The service offered housing security, and the accommodations were conveniently located within a reasonable distance of both the university and the city center.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: As far as I know, there isn't much on-campus housing available in Oslo, but by living in student housing, you're still close to other students. In some accommodations, you can choose to share a kitchen, which is a great way to meet new people. I found the housing to be in good condition overall and was very satisfied with my own accommodation.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Compared to the teaching style I'm used to at the University of Copenhagen, I was very pleased with my experience. I enjoyed both my courses and my instructors, and I felt that, unlike at KU, there was less pressure and fewer unrealistic expectations placed on students regarding how much they could accomplish. It created a more balanced and less stressful learning environment.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I highly recommend exploring places like Frognerseteren and Vettakollen for breathtaking views and hikes. Check out the Deichman Library for its modern architecture, and don't miss the Opera House, where you can walk on the roof for stunning cityscapes. Spend time in St. Hanshaugen and Grünerløkka for cozy cafés, vibrant streets, and a great atmosphere. A walk along the Akerselva river is also a must, as well as visiting the Munch Museum to dive into Norwegian art and culture. And there's so much more to discover—Oslo has something for everyone!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Adjusting to the local culture was very easy. The atmosphere was welcoming, and since there are many similarities between Nordic cultures, it felt natural to settle in. People were friendly, and the city has a relaxed vibe that made the transition smooth and enjoyable.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
If you're going on exchange to Oslo, I've got a few tips for you when it comes to meeting local students! First of all, make sure to join some student organizations or clubs. The university has tons of options, and it's a really easy way to meet people who share your interests. Also, don't skip the social events like parties, cultural evenings, or any activities organized by the university – they're great for breaking the ice.

One thing I found really helpful was joining study groups for my courses. It's a natural way to get to know people, and it helps with coursework too! Also, spend time in the campus cafeteria or common areas – locals hang out there a lot, and it's a good place to strike up a casual conversation.

Even though most people understand danish, learning a few Norwegian phrases is a great way to make the conversation flow.. Don't forget to check out some of the local student hotspots in Oslo, like Grünerløkka or St. Hanshaugen. These are super popular areas for students to hang out and relax.

The most important thing is just to be open and proactive. Don't wait for others to approach you – introduce yourself, ask questions, and show curiosity about their culture.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: nothing

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: What I appreciated most about the culture in Oslo was how people embrace the outdoors and prioritize enjoying life. I loved the tradition of going on hikes in the mountains or forests on Sundays – it's such a refreshing and grounding way to spend the weekend. I also really enjoyed the café culture; people seemed to take their time at bakeries, strolling around the city, and simply relaxing with friends or family. There's a lovely balance between being active and taking the time to unwind, which I found both inspiring and comforting.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be Prepared for Housing Arrangements: Most exchange students use SiO, which manages student housing in Oslo. It's a great option because it's reliable, the accommodations are well-maintained, and they're usually close to the university and city center. Apply as early as possible, and if you want to meet other students, consider choosing housing where you can share a kitchen.

2. Embrace the Outdoor Lifestyle: Norwegians love spending time in nature, and you'll have incredible opportunities to explore it too. Whether it's hiking to places like Vettakollen or Frognerseteren, or taking a stroll along Akerselva, make sure to take advantage of Oslo's amazing outdoor spaces. Pack some good walking or hiking shoes – you'll need them!

3. Plan Your Courses and Schedule Carefull: Check the course catalog and schedules thoroughly to make sure your courses don't overlap, especially with exams. The university provides detailed information about each course, including exam formats and timetables, so use it to your advantage. The system is straightforward, and you can usually get all the courses you want if you plan ahead.

Bonus tip: Take part in the introduction week! It's a fantastic way to meet both local and international students and get settled into life in Oslo. Also, don't hesitate to reach out to the university administration if you have any questions – they're super helpful!
